utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is open. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's IT-01-47-T against General Hadzihasanovic and Brigadier Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Matthias Neuner, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask for the appearances for the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour; good morning, Mr. President. For General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, chief counsel; Mr. Bourgon, co-counsel; and we've got a legal assistant and our case manager here with us as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and our legal assistant Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. On this 219th day of the trial, I would like to welcome everybody present; the Prosecution, the Defence, and General Hadzihasanovic and General Kubura. I would also like to welcome all the other staff assisting us in our task and who have been assisting us in the course of the entire trial, such as the registrar, the legal officers, and the interpreters and the security staff. As to the time at our disposal, following our considerations we have seen that the Defence is left with 49 minutes. Since the Defence had six hours and now the Defence can also -- the Prosecution used six hours, and now the Defence had the right to six hours as well and they're left with 49 minutes. It is nine minutes -- seven minutes past nine, so you have until 9.56, almost 10.00, in order to conclude with your closing arguments. So now I'd like to give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, this is almost the end of a very long trial which went on, as you've already mentioned, for 219 days. I still have several things left to tell you, but for once - and this is a promise now - I'm going to make an effort and keep it brief and not use up the entire 49 minutes that you have been so kind as to allocate to us. In the course of the remaining few minutes, Mr. President, I'm first of all going to deal very swiftly with three preliminary issues before I move on to talk about the theory which has been proposed here in the course of this trial, and then in the end I'm going to briefly refer to all the measures that had been implemented by General Hadzihasanovic in 1993 in order to live up to his responsibilities as the commander of the 3rd Corps as well as to live up to his legal obligations. Afterwards, my colleague will take the floor and give you a brief conclusion and we will not overrun the time that has been allocated to us. First of all, my first preliminary comment: Yesterday, my colleague referred to our arguments as to the detention centres. It goes without saying that in as far as the events at Hotel Sretno are concerned as well as the events at Orasac, in both of these cases our position is the one that we have outlined in our closing brief, that is to say that General Hadzihasanovic never had any knowledge of those events. The second preliminary topic, Mr. President, has to do with the witness statement by Hajrudin Hubo. I had forgotten to mention it yesterday. The Prosecution argued against the credibility of that witness on the basis of a document that had been used in order to jog his memory. More specifically, the exhibit P950. Technically speaking, Mr. President, this exhibit, P950, is a document the use of which is simply restricted to jogging a witness's memory. As a consequence, the content of that document can't be considered as a piece of evidence, so that settles the matter. However, Mr. President, you know us and we are not in the habit of hiding behind technicalities and we always prefer to deal with the topics openly, and on that occasion the witness had explained that that was a document drawn up in 1995 on the basis of the information which was gathered in 1995 and that the contents of that document don't reflect the facts of the matter at all. In other words, there were no foreign El Mujahid members or there were no members in the El Mujahid unit who were also members of the Bosnian armed forces in 1993, and our explanation, Mr. President, is that the person who provided that information to this witness actually made sure that certain members of El Mujahid could obtain Bosnian nationality according to a legal decree from 1993, and here I'm referring to DH994 as well as the report of the constitutional expert Trnka in paragraph 54. That document, Mr. President, establishes through the witness Hajrudin Hubo in 1995 on the basis of the information that he had not actually checked as to the truthfulness of that information, and so this does not actually reflect the actual situation on the ground in 1993. As has already been done on a number of other occasions having argued against the credibility of this witness, the Prosecution actually then based their assumptions on the statement of that very witness. So to say the least this is rather surprising. The other preliminary topic, the official document drawn up by the Economic and Social Council of the UN. By way of example, one of these documents is the exhibit P156 that I had forgotten to mention in the beginning of my statement on Wednesday. This document, P156, Mr. President, makes reference to the fact that the government forces are supposed to have participated in the events at Miletici. What we must keep in mind here, Mr. President, is that this document could not exist without an added reference to government forces, because in the absence of such a reference there would be no violation of human rights with regard to the applicable international law, and in that case the Special Rapporteur of the Human Rights Commission would not actually have any competence there. So we must deal with this document on the basis of the -- not just its content but on the basis of the comments which have led to the drawing up of this document in the first place. In this case, the witness, through a witness statement which was accepted on the Article 92 bis, that is to say it is an internal matter, Rule 92 bis, so they explained the circumstances which had led to the drawing up of this document P156. Last but not least, this is an argument put forward by the Prosecution, that is to say the mention of an event such as Miletici in an international document should imply that the people on the ground knew this. Well, this is an argument which was put forward by the Prosecution, and they have been doing it since the very start, since the very -- since the indictment, and they kept coming back to this throughout the trial. Allow me to put forward another argument, Mr. President. The citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina in a situation of conflict which was raging in their country, well they probably had other things to do rather than read the reports from the Economic and Social Council of the UN. This argument applies to all the UN documents, both military and civilian texts. It is quite certain that as a legal -- as legal experts we view this document as extremely important, and of course it may well happen that we find out about them as soon as they're approved, but for the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, those who were in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993, a report from an Economic and Social Council of the UN, it is certainly not something which is going to draw their attention, to attract their attention as their top priority. And this comes me -- this brings me to the theory I wanted to refer to, the theory put forward by the Prosecution, and I think it is wrong. There are several such theories, but I'm going to deal with the most important ones. The first one, the Prosecution said that the 3rd Corps had to deal with the matter of the Mujahedin on the basis of their obligation to protect the civilian population. We believe, Mr. President, that this is wrong. The responsibility of the 3rd Corps in as far as the protection of the civilians is concerned had to be responsibility recognised on the basis of the domestic law in effect at the time as well as the humanitarian law, the international humanitarian law. In order for this theory to apply in both cases, we can't really deduce such a responsibility of the 3rd Corps with regard to the civilian population. An instrument which could perhaps guide the Trial Chamber there is the first Additional Protocol to the Geneva Convention even though it does not really apply in this case, but there you can read what are the obligations of a commander in as far as the civilian population is concerned, either at the time when the attacks are launched or when he is trying to protect his forces from those attacks. The second theory put forward by the Prosecution, the Mujahedin could not exist as a separate entity in the midst of a conflict such as the one that was raging in Central Bosnia at the time. We believe, Mr. President, that that theory is wrong. Evidence has indicated that not only was it possible but on top of that there were several such groups operating in Central Bosnia and existing quite independently from the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. armed forces. Let me mention another theory put forward by the Prosecution. They claim that General Hadzihasanovic was responsible for the behaviour of all military forces within his area of responsibility. The Defence replies that here, once again, this is a false theory, a wrong theory. The Defence has been able to show that the responsibilities of General Hadzihasanovic could only apply if the elements or the essential conditions of Article 7(3) of the Statute had been met. The fourth theory, the existence or the possibility of an effective horizontal control over the Mujahedin. We believe, Mr. President, that this theory is completely wrong. This has been shown by the Defence as well as our military expert, General Karavelic, who explained very well that -- that an effective horizontal control could not exist. The fifth theory, the control exercised over the civilian authorities in times of war, and this once again with regard to the 3rd Corps is wrong. This has been demonstrated beyond any reasonable doubt by the constitutional expert, both in his report and in the course of his testimony. The sixth theory, the control exercised over deserters and the obligation to going to look for them. There again this is a wrong theory. It has been demonstrated that penal measures could be imposed by the District Military Court with regard to deserters. But it has also been demonstrated that General Hadzihasanovic could not be held accountable for the actions of any such person over whom he no longer had any effective control. Last but not least, the Prosecution put forward the theory that General Hadzihasanovic would have been obliged to attack the Mujahedin in order to sort this out once and for all. Our reply is that this is completely wrong. It has been demonstrated quite clearly that the decision to attack the Mujahedin was not a legal obligation but an operational consideration. On top of that, the need to take on the Mujahedin would make it simply impossible for anyone to think that either General Hadzihasanovic or anyone else in the 3rd Corps could indeed have any control over these forces. And this brings me to the last part of my closing argument, Mr. President, and that is the measures implemented by General Hadzihasanovic. The first statement: Article 7(3) of the Statute does not require a commander to implement all necessary measures but the necessary and reasonable measures. There is an important distinction to be made there. The second statement: Yesterday, I referred to statements made by international, local, military, and civilian witnesses with regard to General Hadzihasanovic. We referred to his character, his motives, his skills, and his personality, his character. It follows, Mr. President, that the character of General Hadzihasanovic as a whole seems to be totally incompatible with the theories put forward by the Prosecution, that is to say that such a person would have neglected to implement certain measures in certain cases. The Prosecution has not even tried to show why such a commander would fail to implement measures in certain cases. The third statement: In his report, General Karavelic has given us a detailed account of responsibilities, obligations, duties, and tasks to be carried out by a perfect and ideal commander. In our closing brief, we gave you a list of everything that General Hadzihasanovic has done and accomplished in order to live up to his responsibilities as the commander of the 3rd Corps. We respectfully submit to you, Mr. President, that everything that has been accomplished by General Hadzihasanovic in this area was simply incompatible with the theory put forward by the Prosecution, that is to say the fact that this commander would have failed to implement reasonable and necessary measures had he been in a position to do so. Once again, the Prosecution has not even tried to explain why such a commander would have failed to implement measures if he had been in a position to do so. The fourth statement: Yesterday, I referred to the type of measures that one can expect from a commander if he knows or has reason to know that a subordinate person was about to commit a crime, or if he -- if he knew about such a crime having been perpetrated. According to the case law of the International Tribunal, but also according to the case law with regard to other war crimes trials after World War II, in our final brief we have explained all the measures implemented by General Hadzihasanovic in line with Article 7(3) of the Statute. We've even added a description of those measures in the annex. There are quite a few of those measures of different kinds, and they touch upon all areas above and beyond of what can be reasonably expected from a general according to the case law. So we respectfully submit, Mr. President, that General Hadzihasanovic went above and beyond the call of duty and above and beyond his obligation and that all this is totally incompatible with the theory put forward by the Prosecution, that is to say that he is supposed to have done everything except in cases of certain violations. The Prosecution has not even tried to show us why -- or not even tried to put forward the reason why such a commander who has implemented so many measures would have failed to live up to his obligations under certain circumstances. It is quite clear, if we look at the evidence, that General Hadzihasanovic in this field, to use a less strict form of words, was more Catholic than the Pope, and for a Muslim it means a great deal. The fifth theory, on a more serious note: We had suggested to the Chamber in what way these measures could be appreciated, and it has to do, for example, with the Yamashita case. It is very weird that the Prosecution has not suggested any such standard against which to measure the measures implemented by the general. Perhaps it's only to be expected because the Prosecution, in trying to avoid from every point of view the use of any context, could have been expected to do so. So in the first place, we need to see whether the commander did act not quite in line with the common practices in terms of commanding. And secondly, "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... supervise that constitutes criminal negligence, plus there must be personal neglect amounting to a wanton, immoral disregard for the actions of his subordinates amounting to acquiescence." [Interpretation] So we respectfully suggest to this Trial Chamber that General Hadzihasanovic's behaviour does not even come close to this sort of behaviour, and on the basis of his exemplary conduct we can see that he acted quite differently in 1993. And this brings me to my last statement, Mr. President, which goes to support everything I have said so far with regard to measures. The Prosecution has not actually provided us with any burden of proof as to this supposed neglect or failure to implement measures. I would first of all like to thank my colleague from the Prosecution, who for longer than 35 minutes explained to us what measures had been implemented by General Hadzihasanovic. For example, in January 1993. I would also like to thank my colleague who on behalf of the Prosecution has tried to minimise the number of measures implemented by General Hadzihasanovic and his military police battalion. In the first case, the arguments put forward by my colleague give us an overview of what was done at all levels of the armed forces in order to combat crime. In the second case, let me respectfully submit to you that one can't really take seriously this argument according to which only 40 per cent of 800 measures, 800 and more, actually concerned the army or the members of the armed forces. The question that imposes itself is that the Prosecution has not been in a position to prove their case. The 800 measures to which they refer in their document are just an overview of things that had been done. The Prosecution was trying to contradict the policy put forward by Mr. Hadzihasanovic when it came to crime. That is to say, what we heard from witnesses was actually zero tolerance. And last -- last year the mission of the -- the Hackshow mission was a failure from every point of view. We can't say that this mission was a success. Quite the contrary, this mission had the totally different effect. This mission made it possible to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that it is not possible to claim that no measures were taken in relation to all of the charges levelled against General Hadzihasanovic. When we examine this more closely, we can see that there are numerous documents in the archives -- numerous archives where we can find documents that concern the counts in the indictment. The evidence shows, Mr. President, that 3rd Corps units also filed complaints or criminal reports with District Military Courts. We haven't seen these documents, Mr. President. If we take Bugojno as an example, we have no documents from the courts that functioned in that town. This is in evidence. But we don't know what was contained in these archives. And similarly, it's too late to provide a new interpretation of Article 6 on the decree on disciplinary measures, although an expert could have addressed this issue if the Prosecution had expressed any doubts. I'd like to remind you that Article 6 states that if the conduct is such that it should be the subject of disciplinary measures and punishment, both should be applied. One does not exclude the other. Such disciplinary measures can be taken in a time of war, and one can stop there or, at an appropriate time, the entire matter could be referred to a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. District Military Court. In our opinion, Mr. President, one cannot claim that a prison sentence of 60 days is not sufficient for the acts referred to in the indictment. Why? Because we are not familiar with the details of the complaints nor are we familiar with the identity of the alleged perpetrators. Mr. President, as an example, I'd like to refer to DH1200. This document is a request for an investigation to be launched. I think it's important to mention the details of the request, and I quote in English: "There are reasonable grounds to believe that [In English] 1993 --" [Interpretation] an important date -- "[In English] returning from the village of Bjelo Buce to Travnik, in order to acquire unlawful gain, he misappropriated two pairs of children's shoes, two children's skirts and one child's fur-lined coat from an abandoned house owned by a local Croat. These items were found and seized by members of the MUP, Travnik SJB, public security station, at the police checkpoint near the Borac factory in Travnik, and hereby committed the crime of aggravated theft under Article 148 ... of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is the kind of army you have to deal with when rendering a decision in this case. The poor soldier who came back from the combat area and passed through an abandoned house and who had children who had nothing to wear, nothing to eat. For his children he stole a fur-lined coat, a skirt, some shoes, and he's accused of a crime before the District Military Court. If people took care to file criminal reports with the military prosecutor in the district of such events, what sort of action do you think he took in other cases? More than a thousand soldiers were prosecuted or criminal reports were filed to prevent these soldiers from committing crimes or to arrest soldiers who had committed crimes. In our trial brief we have said on a number of occasions that the Prosecution has used documents to say that the general was aware of the situation in the field, whereas these documents show beyond any reasonable doubt that as soon as General Hadzihasanovic had a shred of doubt that his troops had been misbehaving, he immediately issued the appropriate orders. And we have explained to you that given the level at which he operated, he could not take his car and go to Travnik and go there to arrest the soldiers with the skirts and the shoes. This is not the role of a corps commander. The role of a corps commander with over 30.000 men under him is to take measures as soon as he hears about such cases, and this is what General Hadzihasanovic did throughout the year 1993. He took such measures, and the Prosecution has failed to prove that such measures were not taken. Let me go back to my example. If I was a commander and I found a soldier of mine who had stolen two pairs of shoes, in the Canadian army, at least, I can tell you that there wouldn't be a criminal report. He would be placed in detention, but this would be a disciplinary measure. When we mention Article 6 and when one says that it's possible for a unit commander to take disciplinary measures and to place people in detention and this is what was done, well, there are various types of events, various types of crimes or offences for which measures were taken, including up to 60-day detention period. We have explained all of this in detail in our final trial brief, and for this reason the lack of evidence to show that measures were taken means that General Hadzihasanovic should be acquitted on all counts. It's not sufficient to say that the parties have visited the archives. The Prosecution had the burden of proof and they have failed to prove their case. I could mention all the archives that haven't even been visited, the local police stations, the security centres, the Cantonal Courts, the Municipal Courts. All of these places could have yielded the necessary evidence. The difficulty is that we haven't understood the particular nature of this case. That does not concern crimes committed pursuant to 7(1). One is accused of not having taken the appropriate measures. This has to be proved. We have to prove that no such measures were taken, and, Mr. President, this is something that has not been done and this is something that has not been proved. The contrary has been proven by the Defence. I could go on for a very long time, but I'll satisfy myself by saying that proving something beyond any doubt is to prove something beyond any reasonable doubt. Penal law, criminal law is simple. It requires rigor and there has been no demonstration of rigor in this case. Would it be possible for General Hadzihasanovic to be acquitted of all the charges in this case? This must be possible, Mr. President, and this is the reason for which we have trials. We submit that General Hadzihasanovic should not have been accused. I invite you to examine objectively the charges levelled against Plavsic, Kordic, Brdjanin, Stakic, Krstic and others. If we just have an objective examination of the sort of charges levelled at them, at the involvement of these individuals, naturally these charges are just allegations until it has been proven, but we are talking about the involvement of high-level individuals, high-level individuals involved in numerous murders. And this has nothing to do with this case. There were numerous victims in that case. Why has General Hadzihasanovic been accused? It's because of the Mujahedin, that's what I said. That a trial that goes on for 219 days has not -- has an objective establishing of the existence of al Qaeda. The Prosecutor could have called someone to testify about al Qaeda but they didn't do this because they know that an expert would have said that this is the sort of person who never places himself under the control of anyone. These sort of people act independently, and this is what they did in 1993. Was General Hadzihasanovic accused because the Prosecutor wants a balance of charges in the course of these conflicts? Is he trying to respond to the criticism that not only the Serbs and the Croats committed crimes? Is he trying to respond to the charge that Muslims also committed crimes? We have to mention this because my -- because when this trial was opened, the first thing my colleague said was not that he was here to establish the responsibility of a general. He said, "We are here to show you the other side of the coin, to show that crimes were committed by the other side too." This is not the objective of this trial. The objective of this trial is not to show that Muslims committed crimes. Everyone knows that. All the observers in the field know that all of the parties to the conflict committed crimes. But everyone also knows that crimes were not committed at the same level, and they know that the individuals responsible were not at the same level. Everyone knows that crimes have to be attacked if they are established, but one should not proceed in a random manner. One should not select a commander, choose him to be a symbol, and say, "Look, the Muslims are just as responsible as the Serbs and the Croats." That is not justice. Mr. President, we believe that the Chamber will not be influenced by such indirect pressure, but these things have to be stated openly. This Tribunal was established to re-establish peace and security, for the sake of reconciliation between the peoples, and false reconciliation based on alleged crimes that doesn't reflect the situation in the field cannot result in reconciliation. Having examined all the evidence, we are certain that the only conclusion that you'll be able to draw is that General Hadzihasanovic should be acquitted on all of the counts against him. And to conclude, Mr. President, there is a document I would like to file, a document that was provided to us by the commander of the UN Detention Unit. It's a document that you are familiar with because, mistakenly, our request to the Registrar to obtain a report on General Hadzihasanovic's conduct in the detention unit, by mistake, this report was sent to the Chamber. We wrote a letter for the Registrar and we asked for a report from the detention unit commander with regard to the accused and this letter was provided to the Chamber by mistake. The contents of the letter are excellent, but we expected a lot more. I spoke to the detention unit commander, and he told me that he would write a report on the conduct of General Hadzihasanovic. It's a good report. We'll take this opportunity to file it. There are three paragraphs here. And although the three paragraphs are not what we expected, nevertheless they do prove that the behaviour of Mr. Hadzihasanovic was exceptional throughout his period of detention, and it tallies with everything that we have said. And finally, Mr. President, I would like to apologise for the vigour with which I have been engaged in this case on occasion. It's the most difficult thing for a lawyer, to represent someone who is innocent. The pressure that a lawyer feels when representing someone who is innocent, Mr. President, is something we have had to live with for several months now. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to conclude our submissions today, our closing arguments on the 219th day of the trial of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, an ABiH commander, I would like to say that the last words uttered by my colleague are words that have been present with us throughout this trial. We have done our best to demonstrate to you by using evidence, by using written evidence, by using witnesses we have called, for you to arrive at the same conclusion, because all the evidence that has been presented to this Trial Chamber shows only one Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. thing: That you have before you an honest, professional soldier, a commander who acted in impossible conditions and did the impossible in order to create an army, to discipline an army, to create a feeling of respect for the law among his soldiers and to punish all those who failed to respect the law. As my colleague has said, and this is what we have already mentioned in our trial brief, unfortunately the Prosecutor is advancing theories which take us back to the beginning of the trial. It is not only that he is erroneously referring to certain locations, the Prosecutor is going back to documents that the Prosecutor wants to use to show that General Enver Hadzihasanovic was responsible for everything that happened in the area where he acted as commander. You are again shown P363, the rules on the law of war of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia. Although their expert, their military expert Reinhardt responded to the following question: "What would you say if we said that those rules of the war law in the SFRY were not adopted in Bosnia?" General Reinhardt responded: "Then my assumption is erroneous. It was my assumption that those rules and those part of the rules were the applicable law in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina." In response to the following question: "Did you come across any laws or rules that were in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina according to which a commander is responsible for everything that take place in his area of responsibility?" And the general, General Reinhardt, responded and said: "That was the main question. I didn't find anything else. That was a key document. So that is what is at stake. I really made a mistake. I have to change my position because it was erroneous at the outset." It's as if the Prosecution did not listen to the evidence in this case but stood by his position. Your Honours, we don't ask you to believe us, but in this case in which you have allowed us to call numerous witnesses, in which you have allowed us to cross-examine the Prosecution witnesses, we ask you to examine the evidence that has been presented, and having done so, establish what the case is. The Defence claims that you have before you a reasonable and responsible commander who always did not only what he was supposed to do in accordance with the law, but he went beyond that, and for this reason we are asking you to acquit General Hadzihasanovic on all counts in the indictment. As his Defence lawyer and for the entire Defence team, it has been very difficult to defend General Hadzihasanovic, although we have had the honour to do so before this Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now give the floor to the Prosecution that agrees with the Defence if they want to add something that concerns the location. It's not really a response. It's an additional piece of information that the Prosecution would like to provide. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This is a brief response to some arguments, not really legal response but in response to something raised by the Hadzihasanovic Defence and which the Kubura Defence spoke with us about earlier. Your Honours will recall that in our final trial brief and in our oral submissions we made reference to three documents which I will mention in a moment relating to Orasac. These documents and the discussion of them are described in paragraphs 134 and 258 of the Prosecution's final trial brief. The documents concerned are Exhibits P500, P501, and P611. These documents -- excuse me. These documents are specifically referred to in footnotes 414, 418, 839, and 879. Upon further consideration of the context contained within those documents and in light of the maps that were shown to the Trial Chamber at the beginning of the Hadzihasanovic oral arguments, the Prosecution is no longer arguing that the Orasac referred to in these three exhibits as described in the paragraphs and footnotes that I have just mentioned is the same Orasac where the alleged detention and beheading of Mr. Popovic occurred. To be absolutely clear, Your Honours, we are no longer claiming that the Orasac mentioned in these documents is the same Orasac that is described in the indictment. All other aspects with respect to the events in Orasac, both as described in our final trial brief and in our oral submissions, remain the same. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have taken note of what you have just said. It's five to ten. We have another 35 minutes before the break. Would Brigadier Kubura's Defence like to start now or would you prefer to have the break? As you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I think, with Your Honour's leave, we will commence now so we can get under way as soon as possible and then take our break at 10.30 and continue thereafter. Your Honours, on behalf of Mr. Kubura, we will be short in closing his case as there is, in our submission, not very much at all to answer despite the fact that these proceedings have commenced some four years ago for Mr. Kubura, in 2001, a long time in anybody's life. Having now reviewed the Prosecution's brief, and most importantly having heard their oral submissions at the beginning of this week, there is, in our view, very little that requires a reply from Mr. Kubura, especially in relation to the killings in Miletici and Maline, where the 7th Brigade was virtually not mentioned at all in the Prosecution's closing oral submissions. Indeed, Your Honours, the Prosecution have not squarely and with clarity and confidence laid the blame for those killings at the doorstep of Mr. Kubura. Considering what we have all heard, Your Honours, over the past few days, in our submission it is to the Prosecution's credit that they end their case on this note. They are not, in fact, seeking to stretch the evidence a bridge too far. The Prosecution is in fact ending at a point different to the one they might have set out to achieve when they opened this case at the end of 2003. The reality is that the Prosecution is not certain of its case against Mr. Kubura for Miletici and Maline, and our primary submission is that Your Honours cannot be certain either. He must be acquitted of these killings. Your Honours found a case to answer in respect of these killings when we submitted our 98 bis motion, but as Your Honours indicated in your decision, once we go beyond the end of the Prosecution case, the standard of proof is then raised to one of beyond reasonable doubt. And even though there might have been a case to answer, it does not mean that the case has been proved to the requisite level of beyond reasonable doubt. Your Honours will, of course, appreciate that beyond reasonable doubt means certainty. It means Your Honours have to be sure before a conviction can be entered. Where there is any doubt, an acquittal must follow. This is the golden thread that runs through all of international criminal law and indeed all of our domestic jurisdictions. It is based on the cornerstone principle of the presumption of innocence. Guilt can only be assigned to an individual where it is proved without any doubt that the person committed those crimes. The Prosecution have maintained their request to Your Honours, albeit, in our submission, a weakened one, that Your Honours convict Mr. Kubura for the killings. But there is no firmness, no lucidity in the evidence and arguments that are presented by the Prosecution against Mr. Kubura. There is no trusty structure, we say, for Your Honours to hold onto. To draw on a well-known image, the Prosecution's case is a bit like a giant sponge which has been absorbing streams of water from all directions, but it is now leaking and dripping at every corner. The Prosecution has been trying to fill in the gaps to stop the leaking by either downplaying to some extent Mr. Kubura's role, as I've mentioned already, or by putting aside evidence that could be -- that could be relevant, that is on the record, or by overlooking points that are raised by the Defence, or by seeking to draw inferences and conclusions in a circumstantial case that are quite simply unsustainable and in some instances unfair to Mr. Kubura. We say in many critical areas their case is riddled with what might be termed pyramiding of inferences, which is drawing an inference upon another inference upon another inference upon another inference, piling one on top of the other in a drive to get a legal conclusion of guilt at any cost. It goes without saying that the Prosecution of war crimes is a very serious matter, the Prosecution having been mandated by the Security Council of the international community to prosecute those most responsible for the commission of serious - and I underline serious - violations of international humanitarian law. Accusations made in indictments cannot be taken lightly. These are public documents for the entire international community. So when, firstly, for example, the Prosecution alleges in the indictment at paragraph 27 that in June 1993 there was a massive attack by the Bosnian army during which 200 civilians were killed, we have to consider very carefully whether that allegation has been made out. In our submission, there is no evidence to prove that Mr. Kubura was involved in a massive attack where 200 civilians were killed in a relatively short period of time. And if this fact hasn't been proved, and comparatively speaking the casualties are much, much lower during that time period, is this not a factor that Your Honours can take into account as mitigation? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The Prosecution have indicated that there is no mitigation in this case. However, in the Blaskic appeal, the Appeals Chamber noted very clearly that the circumstances of the conflict and the role of the accused before, during, and after the conflict is a mitigating factor, bearing in mind as well whether there was a discriminatory, clear discriminatory basis for actions undertaken. Secondly, Your Honours, there is the assertion made in the Prosecution's written closing brief, and this is at page 4, and this concerns the foreigners or Mujahedin. It's the first time that they raise the issue. Paragraph 9, which goes over to page 4, and they say: "... the mere presence and employment in combat of the Mujahedin during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina casts serious doubts on the sincerity of the Bosnian army's stated goal of maintaining a secular and multi-ethnic Bosnia where all nationalities could live peacefully." Your Honour, I should make it clear that in our submission these matters have very little to do with the charges in the indictment, which I will come on to, but as a public document the indictment and the allegations that are made by the Prosecution must be carefully scrutinised. In our submission, this kind of statement is far overstated. From the very first case that was heard before the ICTY, the Tadic case, the Prosecution has called evidence from experts like Dr. James Gow, and in their submissions have emphasised that the perspective of the Bosnian government and its armed forces was for a multi-ethnic solution to the future of that country. That continued in the Kupreskic case, in the Blaskic case, in the Kordic case. I recall the evidence of another expert, Professor Robert Donia, relied on by the Prosecution in those cases. And indeed, the very spirit of the Dayton agreement is driven by the multi-ethnic principle. Perhaps again, Your Honours, these background circumstances may be ones which count as mitigating in this case. Thirdly and most importantly in respect of the charges against Mr. Kubura, the Prosecution have still not presented a clear case in respect of Mr. Kubura as to how he effectively controlled the Mujahedin who were involved in any of the crimes alleged in the indictment. The Prosecution's brief is now littered with the phrase "Mujahedin were incorporated within the 3rd Corps, including - including - the 7th Brigade." Your Honours will recall how when we opened the case for Mr. Kubura we noted four separate indictments that had preceded this case and that had come out during this case, each with a different approach to what was the relationship between the Mujahedin and the 7th Brigade as the Prosecution puts it. We now have a different and to some extent a new formulation, which is that the Mujahedin were included in units including the 7th Brigade. It mirrors in many ways what is in the indictment against Mr. Delic. But the lingering questions remain. They still have not been answered. Who exactly does the Prosecution say was included in the 7th Brigade and when? And most importantly for this case, were they the perpetrators? The Prosecution have not been able to, in their final attempts here before Your Honours closing the case, answer any of those questions to give Your Honours any certainty to proceed with. Instead, what the Prosecution seeks is a guilty verdict on the basis of the following assertions: They say, first of all, we accept Mr. Kubura was not the de jure commander. He didn't have those powers. But he was a de facto commander of the entire brigade. They then go on to say that some foreigners, we can't say which but some, were subordinated to the 7th Brigade. Not a horizontal association or cooperation, they were actually subordinated; they were within your brigade. They then go on to allege that certain foreigners were involved in committing killings in Miletici and Maline. They can't say which other than they came from the Mehurici camp. They were foreigners from there. They then start to try to link it all together by saying as a de facto commander, in the case of Miletici for only less than two weeks, of the 7th Brigade, you must have controlled the particular foreigners that were in Mehurici that committed the crimes. And moreover, you must have known about all of those offences while they were being committed or afterwards. There's not a single sentence in their brief about knowledge, what is the evidence that proves that Mr. Kubura knew about these offences. It's merely an asserted fact. And then drawing all that together, the Prosecution then set aside all the evidence and the documents and the war diaries that show that the 7th Brigade was not present in those locations. That's simply not addressed as another potential rational explanation for what occurred on those days, and they say Your Honours must find him guilty of murder. Those are the hoops, seven of them, that they ask Your Honours to go through in order to convict. We say that no reasonable trier of fact could ever convict on the basis of those assertions and the links that the Prosecution seeks to make between them. There is no basis for a conviction. I want to here make a comment about measures which Mr. Mundis spent some time on at the end of the Prosecution's oral submissions. Your Honour will recall that General Reinhardt in his evidence confirmed that the issue of measures only arises once you have established that the perpetrators are indeed the subordinates of the commander and that the commander knew or had reason to know what they were doing. Once that is established, it then has to be considered, well, what did the commander do? Was it enough, reasonable and necessary in the circumstances? Mr. Mundis is absolutely correct in highlighting the importance of measures to this case. In respect of Mr. Kubura, the only time that that issue may arise, we say, is for the alleged crimes in Vares, which I will come to address in due course. But for all of the other offences, he was either not the commander, not in effective control of the perpetrators because they were not his subordinates, or there's no evidence that he knew or had reason to know about the offences. And it's for that reason that Your Honours will be fully aware that the issue of measures has not been a part of Mr. Kubura's Defence. You cannot take measures if people are not your subordinates, if you don't know that crimes have been committed. In Vares, yes, Mr. Kubura was present. Your Honours have heard evidence of that. And in our submission, he did take measures appropriate to what his subordinates were doing. In highlighting measures or repression of crimes, Mr. Mundis was also correct in emphasising the plight of victims in Central Bosnia. We all agree that those responsible must be punished for the sake of justice, for the sake of the grieving families of victims who remain behind. This trial has provided some of them with an opportunity to come before Your Honours and tell their stories, to make them public, and in at least some way, perhaps a greater way for some of those persons, that in itself would have contributed to the healing process and, more broadly, to reconciliation on the basis that the suffering has not been forgotten. All we ask is that in the context of a criminal trial the real proven perpetrators, at whatever level they might be, are those held responsible. We do the victims no service to blame the wrong persons, and we do the delicate process of building a new unity no service to stretch evidence, to build inference upon inference in an effort to find someone responsible at any cost. Your Honours, I will now move on to two charges that the Prosecution have paid great attention to in their oral submissions. In fact, those are the charges they have made most of the assertions about the 7th Brigade, those being the Motel Sretno and Vares. In reality, these are instances which lasted no more than one day each. We wish to respond to the particular assertions that have been made by the Prosecution in respect to each of those. I will not be repeating what is in our written brief. Our aim is to try to, where the Prosecution have explained their theory, explain whatever evidence they rely upon, to respond directly to that for each of those counts. We will be referring to our written brief and to some documents, but there is no need for Your Honours to have those documents before you, and we will not have any further computer aids. Your Honours, perhaps before I start with the Motel Sretno, that would be a good time to have our first break, and I will commence there immediately afterwards. Thank you, Your Honours.
