utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Motel Sretno. The Prosecution bases the case against Mr. Kubura for the charges for Motel Sretno on him being present, they say, in Kakanj on the 18th of May, 1993, and there are two pieces of evidence that they rely upon to draw this conclusion. Firstly, there's P562, which is a document from the 7th Brigade indicating that certain persons must go to Dusina, and they connect that with document P563, which is one signed on the 18th of May by the duty operations officer which states that the chief of staff, together with others, is in the 3rd Battalion. That's the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. documentary evidence. And secondly, they rely upon the statement of a victim who heard the name Kubura being mentioned by an HVO commander at a meeting a day later chaired by the French UNPROFOR officer. This, Your Honours, is classic circumstantial case that the Prosecution puts, using inferences to try to reach a particular conclusion. It should be compared with the kind of circumstantial case they seek to use for Miletici and Maline. In our submission, their efforts cannot even be called a circumstantial case. It doesn't fall within the realm of what one would call a classic attempt to prove a legal conclusion through various inferences. The assumption for Motel Sretno is that the document P563 reflects the truth of the situation as the Prosecution put it. They ask Your Honours to infer that the chief of staff referred to there is Mr. Kubura, that the document is correct in saying that he was in the 3rd Battalion, and that the meaning of "in the 3rd Battalion" is "in the Motel Sretno." In addition, they ask Your Honours to infer that the reference to Kubura by the witness must be to Mr. Amir Kubura and that he was, therefore, in the area a day later, that he therefore knew and that he therefore had the ability to act, but because he didn't do so, he's criminally responsible. There's also another, as a footnote, inference that they ask Your Honours to draw in that they say a 7th Brigade guerrilla unit participated in the events because certain witnesses noted persons who arrested them wearing headbands, and therefore they ask Your Honours to infer that it must have been a guerrilla unit of the 7th Brigade. In our submission, this is also a classic case of inference pyramiding, piling one inference upon the other. The reason why we say that is that if Your Honours take document P563, the Prosecution has led no evidence to prove that the contents of that document are indeed correct. That document, we have checked the transcripts, was never shown to a single witness, so its contents was never tested before Your Honours by any persons who were there at the time. What Your Honours do have is the oral evidence of Mr. Alajbegovic who said, and I quote, at page 18697, when he was asked: "Do you know whether on that day or later on Mr. Kubura stayed in Kakanj,?" That date being the 18th of May. He said, "Amir Kubura didn't stay in Kakanj on that day or the following day. He did not appear in the barracks where we were." He was then asked: "You say he didn't appear in the barracks on that day. As a rule when somebody from the command brigade in Zenica came to the barracks, would the battalion command be aware of that fact or was some other procedure followed?" And he said: "Well, usually, the battalion command would be aware of the fact that somebody from the brigade command was coming. It wouldn't be possible for someone to come in secret without having announced his visit." So you have oral testimony there, Your Honours, that directly contradicts what is written on the face of that document P563. I would also refer Your Honours to the testimony of Mr. Kulovic, at page 18812, who confirmed the same. In our submission, Your Honours, there must therefore be reasonable doubt as to whether that document is accurate. The Prosecution never ever suggested to either of those witnesses that they were lying. I think to this day they're not saying that those witnesses are not telling the truth. Indeed, Your Honours might think that if they had fabricated the entire story, they would have also said more about where Mr. Kubura might have been. Instead, they gave, in our submission, very straightforward answers. They didn't see him on that day, and it would be most unusual for somebody from the brigade command to be there without them knowing. That evidence alone must raise a doubt, in our submission. The Prosecution has sought to argue that military documents like P563 are inherently reliable. So they would argue Your Honours can take what is written in 563 as the gospel truth without hearing any witness, without hearing from the author of the document, with any corroboration whatsoever. In our view, military documents are like all other documents. There's nothing special about them. Each and every document that Your Honours consider has to be looked at on its own merits, whether it comes from the military or a private individual or a government. There's no reason why the military are likely to be more accurate than anybody else. In fact, quite the contrary. At paragraph 12 of the Prosecution brief, they say because military documents relate to very serious matters, including matters of life and death, accuracy is therefore important. But Your Honours might think equally when documents involve life and death issues, who is to blame or whose fault it is, that there's every reason to fabricate documents, that there's every reason to be inaccurate under the pressures and strains of war. These were not normal times. Perhaps an accountant can be faulted for making an error when sitting in his or her office preparing books over a long period of time under little pressure, but surely the same cannot be said of those involved in the heat of battle. In our submission, Your Honours, there are an equal number of reasons why military documents may not be inherently reliable and that each and every document therefore has to be looked at very carefully as to whether or not there is evidence independent of the document which supports it. On this point, Your Honour, I do wish to refer Your Honours to a very recent decision that has come out in the Milosevic case. It's a decision dated 8 July 2005, and there the Trial Chamber held, and I will quote this to Your Honours: "The practice of the Trial Chamber has been to deny admission of a document put to a witness where the witness did not adopt or rejected outright or was not in a position to say anything meaningful about the document or an assertion based thereon, on the basis that such a document lacks probative value." Your Honours, I appreciate that all of these documents have been admitted, which is a different approach to that taken by the Trial Chamber in the Milosevic case, but where we are all in agreement is that the critical issue is what value should now be attached to those documents. This dicta from the Milosevic Trial Chamber, in our submission, is pertinent to the issue in that it has recognised that the value to be attached to documents which witnesses have not been able to say anything meaningful about is limited. This was indeed the approach that Your Honours took in calling the only witness that Your Honours did call in this case, Witness ZP, in order that he be shown various documents to test the accuracy of the contents or to further explain the contents of those documents. And in some cases he said they were an accurate reflection. In others, he raised question marks or he added further clarifications which were important to understand the true meaning of the document. Your Honours, in our submission, that argument applies very much to document P563 as well. Moving on to the other piece of evidence, the reference to the name "Kubura." Here we have another situation where Your Honours are left with a piece of evidence over which there is doubt. Who is this person being referred to? The Prosecution ask you to infer that it is Mr. Amir Kubura, but what else have they got to point you in that direction? They would say document P563. There are witnesses in that argument, as I've outlined. But in addition to that, they have not called any other evidence to explain who was at that meeting. Here you have a meeting of UNPROFOR with HVO commanders. Was the burden not on the Prosecution to find witnesses who were there and to confirm one way or the other who was at that meeting? The witness who we are referring to at page 2126, he said when he was asked in cross-examination that he didn't know anyone at this meeting. He said he couldn't say who the name Kubura referred to, whether he was an ordinary soldier or an officer. He concluded by saying: "I'm afraid it is very difficult for me to say who was there." So Your Honours are left with a situation where you don't have a positive identification. Where there is doubt, in our submission it must be given to the accused. He must receive the benefit of those uncertainties. It is for the Prosecution to construct a coherent and thorough case using all the resources at their disposal. As Your Honours have indeed noted, it was incumbent upon the Prosecution to make it clear to the Trial Chamber what the structure of the army was at the time. Who were the different commanders at the different levels in the brigades and the battalions within those brigades and leading up to the corps command? The Prosecution had the burden of establishing what the links were between these various people, how documents and reports were exchanged, and ultimately when it comes to the charges, who was present at what times and in what capacities. That is surely the basis of any case brought under Article 7(3). The Prosecution is the engine that drives this case. It was for the Prosecution to find, as it could have, in our submission, the potentially direct evidence on many of these points which would have assisted Your Honours in determining what is the truth. We say instead what you're left with are bits and pieces of evidence, shades of grey which are plagued with doubt. You do not have the certainty, we say, to convict on that basis. Your Honour, if I may pause here and use the opportunity to make some submissions on the nature of circumstantial evidence which are relevant not only to Motel Sretno but also to the other charges that I'm Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. going to come on to discuss. Any legal dictionary will indicate that circumstantial evidence can be defined as any fact from the existence of which the judge may infer the existence of a fact in dispute. But there are always two cautions that are outlined in the use of circumstantial evidence, and it is the Prosecution that have maintained that their case is based largely on circumstantial evidence. These two cautions must apply, we say: First of all, as the number of steps which you have to take from the first fact to get to the ultimate fact increases, the weaker becomes the first fact as a way, as a means of proving the ultimate fact. If there are a number of steps, the opportunities as well for showing evidence where there is a contrary conclusion increases. Secondly, the common fear that all triers of fact are aware of of untruthful or inaccurate evidence, it applies even more strongly to circumstantial evidence than direct evidence. Circumstantial evidence must always be examined narrowly as the possibilities of error or of manufacturing false evidence and inaccuracy are inherently more prominent. The fundamental test is that where evidence in a trial is circumstantial, before a finding of guilt may be made, the Court must conclude that the circumstances, and they must be individually proven facts -- so for example, if the Prosecution wants to rely on P563, it has to be a proven fact the truth of what is in that document -- were not only consistent with an inference of guilt but also would not lead to any other reasonable inference. So other reasonable inferences have to be excluded. If there is another rational explanation or other inferences that are consistent with innocence, then the inference has not been established beyond reasonable doubt. What must be guarded against is what I've referred to as pyramiding of one assumption on another, and the reason for this is to protect the public against verdicts which are based on conjecture and speculation. Your Honours, I wish to refer to a particular example of inference stacking which was used by the Prosecution to illustrate my point. And this can apply to all -- all of the charges, we say, in the indictment. It concerned the presence of the 7th Brigade in Guca Gora on the 8th of June, 1993. In our submission, there was no need to seek to make such an inference because Mr. Kubura is not charged with anything in Guca Gora, but it may have significance for the way the Prosecution puts their case in respect of Miletici and Maline. It's a long journey the Prosecution seek to take Your Honours on. It starts with a document P474 on the 22nd of May, signed by Mr. Terzic, and goes all the way through to the 8th of June, the allegation then being that the 7th Brigade were involved. The first document by Mr. Terzic was one that was shown to him. Your Honours may recall it consisted of two pages. The first page was signed by Mr. Terzic, stamped by him, and he said, "Yes, I recognise this document." The second page, which contained information about a detachment at Mehurici of 92 persons, was admitted into evidence as a document attached to the first document, but it wasn't signed, and when Mr. Terzic was asked about it, he said that this was not a document which he recognised or which he prepared. He had prepared the first document over his signature. The Prosecution then referred to a later document, the document marked P481 of 27 May 1993. This is, as Your Honours may recall, an unsigned document that no witness was able to comment on as a document which they had authored but which was shown to Mr. Kadic, the assistant for logistics of the 306th Brigade. This document talks about the redeployment of 20 persons from the Mehurici sector to Radojcici village and for those persons from the 1st Company of the 7th Brigade to be resubordinated to the 306th Brigade. And it says that, "Logistical supplies shall be secured through the 306th Brigade." It's issued in the name of "the battalion commander." That's all it says; no name, no signature. Mr. Kadic said - and Your Honours might think that this is instructive - that it would be impossible to issue an order of this nature for a battalion commander to be subordinating persons to another brigade. Such an order could only be issued from a higher authority, logically. He also said that -- and he was the assistant commander for logistics -- that the supplies that are mentioned in this document were not and could not have been secured through the 306th Brigade. So he was able to say that as far as he knew, that order was not implemented, if it was an order at all. In our submission, he casts serious doubt on the validity of this document, which the Prosecution was not able to and did not counteract in any way. And yet the Prosecution continue to say, "Well, accept the truthfulness of this, Your Honours, and place the 7th Brigade or parts of it in Radojcici village around that time." And then they say, "Well, because that village is relatively close, two to three kilometres, from Guca Gora, and there is a videotape which appears to be taken from that direction of that village, you can therefore conclude that members of the 7th Brigade must have been in the area at the time; they were involved in reconnaissance; they were involved in taking that video; and that in fact what you see on the video is reconnaissance that they would have undertaken before the 8th of June, and then they must have been there on the 8th of June. Because they were involved in reconnaissance, then they must have been there. Your Honour, that, in our submission, is an example of how you take one piece of evidence which is not proven, we say, and seek to stack it on top of other evidence over and over again, stretching it further and further to reach a conclusion where you have no evidence to in fact prove the conclusion directly. In our submission, these are not links in a chain, and this is certainly not a rope - which is often the image used for circumstantial evidence - it's not a rope to be trusted if one was on the edge of a cliff. Your Honour, I'm now going to move on to the charges in respect of Vares, November 1993. The Prosecution commences their case by indicating that there was a context of revenge. There was the massacre in Stupni Do, and they indicate that emotions were running high. But what then, having raised that, is the evidence that there was any revenge? There's been no allegation of any killings or detention or inhumane treatment in respect of anything that happened in Vares. The allegation is one of looting and destruction. In our submission, there are four things the Prosecution has to prove in respect of Vares. They have to prove to Your Honours what exactly was stolen, then by whom, when did that happen - timing is very important - and where was it taken to? Destruction is a separate matter I will come to at the end. For the time being I will focus on the four questions concerning looting. Your Honour, the legal framework within which to consider the question of looting as crime under international humanitarian law is that which prohibits the plunder of property but with the important exception that has always been recognised, that an adverse party may seize military and related equipment belonging to the other party. I refer here, Your Honours, to an extensive survey that has recently been undertaken by the International Committee of the Red Cross, regarded widely as the guardian of international humanitarian law, where they surveyed the practices of the countries of the world, national cases, as well as international cases as well, in an effort to crystalise what the customary law position was on various topics. And in respect of war booty, they noted that the definition is one that is far from clear and in fact includes many items which might not at first glance be incorporated. They noted in defining what was military and related equipment - and I'm quoting here from the chapter in the report at pages 173 to 176 - that it includes arms and ammunition, depots of merchandise, machines, instruments and even cash which belonged to the adversary. But it also includes private property which is actually used for hostile purposes, and some examples are given. Of course arms and ammunition, but also means of transport, stores and supplies, cash, funds, and all property belonging to the state which may be used for military operations. The report then goes on to look at the situation from various countries to show the range of different forms of property that are included. And, Your Honours, given the composition of Your Honours' Trial Chamber, I will cite from certain particular countries. First of all, there's the French military manual which says that, "Military objects from the enemy de facto become war booty, including arms, combat transports and vehicles. The only exception is that sufficient food must be allowed to be available for captured persons." The military manual for Madagascar states that "Captured military objects may become war booty. It may be used without restriction but it belongs to the capturing power and not to individuals." And the military manual of the Netherlands provides that: "Military material, in the first place weapons and ammunition but also other goods destined for military use, including stored goods, may be captured as well." It does indicate that medical goods and goods necessary to feed protected prisoners should not be captured. But there's no dispute in this case that there were no prisoners captured in Vares. There was no need to keep food or goods for any prisoners of the HVO or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. civilians who were there. Your Honours, I raise this legal framework in order to point out that it's for the Prosecution to prove to Your Honours what goods were in fact stolen, do they fit into the category of war booty or not, and then, what happened to them? If they were goods that could have been captured and they were kept by the military, well, according to the customary law position, there's no crime. They have to show that the property was indeed private, totally unconnected to military activities, and that it was taken by individuals and kept by them. This is not just a case of saying: Well, Your Honours, it appears that some houses were looted and it seems that one of the brigades that was there was the 7th Brigade, therefore you can infer that they must have taken some goods, therefore you can infer Mr. Kubura knew, he didn't punish them; he must be guilty. They have to do a proper and precise job. Looting, of course, is not the most serious offence, but if it is alleged against an accused in a public document, then the law must be applied properly. Where is the evidence of what precise goods were stolen, that they had no connection to military activities, that they were taken by individuals to their homes, never to be returned? The Prosecution in their closing submissions relied upon document P676, which says everything is being looted as a piece of evidence to attempt to prove to Your Honours that looting was taking place. There are two problems with it, we say, Your Honours. Firstly, it's a document that goes from the operational group commander to the 6th Corps Command and the 3rd Corps Command. It's not a document that goes to the 7th Brigade. Your Honours might recall this is a document I asked General Reinhardt about in cross-examination, and he said, ah, Mr. Kubura should have known about instances of looting. There was this document that said everything is being looted. And I put to him, well, this document never went to Mr. Kubura. Would you accept that if it hadn't gone to him he wouldn't have known about the contents of it? And he confirmed that. Secondly, Your Honours, all the document says is that everything is being looted. Yes, perhaps at the time it was impossible for them to list item by item, but at the same time the Prosecution can't rely upon this document to prove that the goods that were being looted did not fall within the category of war booty. What does it mean "everything is being looted"? This document, once again, was one that wasn't shown to any witness. Nobody from the 6th Corps, nobody from the 3rd Corps, nobody from the command of the Tactical Group was called to explain what happened in Vares. It's not as though these people are no longer around. The avenues were open for all of these persons, or those necessary to prove the Prosecution's case, to be called. One final point about this document before I move on, Your Honours, is that it goes on to say that the rest of the soldiers joined in the looting and burning. So it's an allegation that the 7th Brigade entered Vares, everything was being looted, and then it says the rest of the soldiers joined in. Now, this is not an assertion that we as the Defence are accepting, because we challenged the truthfulness or put the Prosecution to the proof of the truthfulness of this document. But on the Prosecution's own document, they concede that there were other soldiers, not only soldiers from the 7th Brigade, involved, which has always been one of our arguments based on the evidence, that there were many units involved in this operation. By its very nature being a tactical group combining various corps and brigades, it's evident that not only the 7th Brigade was there, and we say it's for the Prosecution to prove who stole those goods. It's not enough to merely assert that the 7th Brigade was one of the brigades there. They have to show that members of the 7th Brigade were involved at the time they were there and show that they took those goods unlawfully. But what evidence is there of that? We have the testimony of Hakan Birger who said at page 5384 to 5385 that he did see some soldiers taking chocolate, bread. He mentioned pens, mentioned women's shoes. He said also, though, that the UN food storage was not touched. That's at page 5415. There is no other evidence regarding what goods were stolen. Your Honour, in our submission, if that is all the Prosecution have, we are not in a situation where those acts fall within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal to try the most serious offences. In one of the footnotes in the Prosecution's written brief, they quote the first appeal to be considered by the Tribunal, that of the Tadic interlocutory appeal on jurisdiction, where the requirements of the crimes charged under Article 3 were set out. And the third requirement - this is at paragraph 94 - is that the violation must be serious. That is to say, and I'm quoting now: "It must constitute a breach of a rule protecting important values, and the breach must involve grave consequences for the victim. Thus, for instance, the fact of a combatant simply appropriating a loaf of bread in an occupied village would not amount to a serious violation of international humanitarian law." Although it might fall foul of the particular provision in The Hague regulations, strictly speaking it does, but it does not amount to a serious violation of international humanitarian law. Your Honours, in our submission the evidence that the Prosecution have in respect of looting and its connection to the 7th Brigade is de minimus. They even noted that there was famine in the area at the time, that troops would have been hungry, which Your Honour might appreciate would explain why Mr. Birger saw persons taking food, chocolate, bread. When it comes to Mr. Kubura in respect to Vares, the Prosecution base their case on two main points. The first is that he apparently changed the order and decided to send his troops into Vares. In that way, they ask Your Honours to infer an intent to allow his troops to go there, or knowledge on his part that by going there certain actions might occur in a context of revenge. But, Your Honour, it was not Mr. Kubura who decided to send his troops to Vares. It was the corps commander at the time who ordered him in plain terms, and this is in document P674, to go to Vares. It's at point number 4 of the order, and it reads: "If the conditions are right and the town has been abandoned, organise an attack and liberate Vares. The commander OG East shall command all forces for Vares." So clearly indicating that this is now a matter for the OG East to command, but, "You are to organise an attack and liberate Vares." He cannot be criticised for following the orders of his commander. The next point the Prosecution make is that Mr. Kubura did not - and this is probably the crux of their case - did not send the military police of the 7th Brigade into Vares in the morning and thereafter when it's alleged by the Prosecution that looting was taking place. In our submission, Your Honour, he didn't have to do that because he did more than that. He ordered them to withdraw the very same day. As I've indicated before, he didn't get any of the documents from the Tactical Group about any alleged looting. He went to Majdan Vares along the road, about a kilometre outside of Vares, in the morning. You heard evidence to that effect. And once it was ascertained that the town was abandoned, his troops were automatically ordered to leave. The Prosecution does not dispute that the 7th Brigade remained there any longer. All they're saying is that on that day he should have sent his military police in. But for what reason? There were no reports of looting, the town was abandoned, and he ordered them to return. There was a checkpoint set up. The Prosecution makes some issue over whether that was a brigade checkpoint or civilian police. Whatever it was, there was a checkpoint there consisting of police persons, civilian and military, checking soldiers who were leaving. Mr. Kubura was there at the checkpoint. So was the UN. Your Honours might think that in those circumstances he was fully justified in, at that stage, believing the situation was fully under control, that he could go back to his command in Strezevo and that his troops would be back that night to then be transported out. On this issue of whether we as the Defence should have questioned the international witnesses about this checkpoint and that the failure to do that therefore cast some doubt on the truthfulness of what the witnesses for Mr. Kubura said, Your Honours, in our submission the fact that no questions were put in cross-examination during the Prosecution case cannot in any way diminish what Defence witnesses come and say when they are available for the Prosecution to challenge them. The Prosecution never ever suggested to any of the Defence witnesses that there was no checkpoint. They never challenged them as witnesses who have come to make up that allegation. And in our submission, even though we do not have to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt to you, we have established an evidentiary basis for Your Honours to accept that there was a checkpoint outside of Vares. Moreover, the Office of the Prosecutor does not dispute that on that day units of the 7th Brigade who had been in Vares were retreating, moving out, which means they would have passed through that checkpoint and been observed by the UN personnel there as well. Your Honour, if I may digress at that point, as we are looking at the truthfulness of witness testimony, to make a more general point, which is that in our submission, every witness has to be looked at on his or her own merit when they come here. It does not matter which side they come from, which army they were fighting in. It is for Your Honours to assess Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the truthfulness of their evidence given the questions that they are asked by both of the parties. The Prosecution has suggested in its written brief that Your Honour should treat witnesses from the Bosnian army with great caution. In our submission exactly the same potential reasons why witnesses might conceal information or not be accurate in the evidence that they give applies to those within the HVO or any other military. Any person who has been caught up in a war will come with their particular experiences and the same potential to be truthful, untruthful, accurate, inaccurate. Each witness has to be judged on an individual basis. And as Your Honour Mr. President, before every single witness testified, Your Honour indicated that if there was anything that they weren't certain about, whether it could be incriminating or used against them, they had the right to notify Your Honour about that, and there was a procedure for dealing with it whereby they could give their testimony openly without the fear of it being used against them at some point. Your Honour explained that procedure at length to each and every witness. Your Honour, moving on to destruction, then, in Vares, the evidence has been overwhelming, in our view, that there was no destruction other than a few houses that were already destroyed or burning when the forces from the Bosnian army arrived in Vares. You have heard that from Hakan Birger. You've heard that from Sir Martin Garrod. You've heard that from Rolf Weckesser, and Mr. Henricsson as well. Each of them testified in clear terms that they did not witness any destruction. The only evidence that the Prosecution potentially has is that of the cross-shooting when the 7th Brigade allegedly arrived in the outskirts of the town or the town. There seems to be some unclarity about that, although in our submission that makes little difference either way. The Prosecution is suggesting that everyone knew the town was abandoned, and therefore going in in that way, cross-shooting into windows is a form of unlawful destruction. Well, in our submission that can't be right. Even though there might be implication that a town is abandoned, it's impossible to know when you arrive at a town like Vares only a few weeks after massive military operations in the area, that it is definitely abandoned. You surely have to, as a military, take the necessary precautions when arriving. You can't trust any word that you've heard or indications other than what you see yourself when you're there. And Mr. Birger, who saw this, testified in very clear terms that the operation was done in a professional way, and it only lasted as long as was required. Once he told the commander that the town was abandoned and there was no response to the cross-firing, then it ceased. It wasn't a case of it going on and on, of soldiers going into buildings, kicking down doors, setting them alight. There's no evidence of that whatsoever. In his assessment - and this is at page 5384 to 5385 - Mr. Birger said it had been done in a professional military manner as would be expected of any unit entering a town who was uncertain what was there. Your Honour, the Prosecution have conceded that the destruction has to be on a large scale for it to constitute a war crime. On the evidence that we have, in our submission there is no basis for finding that the destruction was large scale or substantial. On Vares, Your Honours, in a line we have another leaking ship. There are holes all over it. You cannot, in our submission, be certain beyond reasonable doubt of the offences in Vares that are charged against Mr. Kubura. Your Honours, I now wish to move on to the subject of de facto command, and I would request that at that point we could break once that topic has been covered, and thereafter I will return to the charges in Maline and Miletici. As I've said before, these are not charges the Prosecution has gone into any great detail in the oral submissions in respect to Mr. Kubura, but I do wish to use the opportunity to set out what our defence is in relation to those alleged killings. De facto command. Your Honours, when this case commenced, the Prosecution started with the date of 1 January 1993 as the date from which Mr. Kubura should be held responsible for crimes committed. After the decision by the Appeals Chamber on whether or not you had to be the commander at the time offences were committed, the Prosecution then moved the date to 1 April 1993 as the date when Mr. Kubura assumed command or should be held responsible. When you read the Prosecution's written brief now, we have another shift. It's moved from 1 April to -- and this is at paragraph 56 - to 12 April, or at least 12 April. As I said before, only less than two weeks before the events in Miletici. On what basis does the Prosecution now allege that at that time, or more or less at that time Mr. Kubura was suddenly elevated to be the de facto commander? In footnote 134 of their brief, the Prosecution allude to four documents; P916, P816, P410, and P727. Your Honour, we've looked at these documents very carefully, and none of them indicate that at that point in particular Mr. Kubura can be said to have become the commander in fact of the entire 7th Brigade. Yes, one of the documents does say that Mr. Korisic is not available, but it doesn't indicate that Mr. Kubura has either been appointed or that he is now the person in charge. There's nothing about either of those documents from which you can infer effective control of the entire brigade. The Prosecution have conceded, Your Honours, that there is no de jure control over the 7th Brigade. There is no official formal appointment until the 6th of August. We say it's the 6th of August, out of all the dates, that is the correct date from which he did become the commander and assume command functions. Whatever happened before 6 August 1993 is not his concern. Your Honours, we fully accept that de jure control is not the only way in which somebody can be held responsible under 7(3). Of course de facto control is a basis for holding someone responsible. In effect as the commander, the person has stepped into the shoes of the de jure commander. Indeed, in the Blaskic appeal it was made quite clear that simply showing de jure control is not sufficient, because in fact somebody else might be in charge. You need to do both. What we dispute is essentially what we regard as a form of strict liability that has been put forward by the Prosecution. Paragraph 57, they say that there's a military principle which is that the senior officer of a unit is always in command in the absence of the de jure commander. The senior officer is always in command. That can't be right, Your Honours. It must depend on the factual circumstances of the individual involved. It might well be that the senior officer is not the person who takes over command in reality, or he might be one of many people who assumes command. It cannot be right that simply because you're the senior person you therefore must be considered the person with the necessary factual powers to prevent or punish. In addition to that, General Karavelic said in his testimony, and Your Honours might, thinking back on their testimony, regard it as an engaging and spontaneous discussion of the issues at stake, one in which he was able to assist Your Honours greatly as somebody who had been in the military, with military experience, as to what happens when a commander is no longer there, and he was adamant that the position of Mr. Kubura was a very uncertain one, that he would have wanted certainty if he was in his position. And although he couldn't say with any certainty, because he didn't know the exact details, he was able to say as a matter of general theory a commander remains a commander until someone is appointed in his place, and that there might have been many reasons, as often happens, why the next most senior person wasn't appointed, why there was a vacuum for a period. But he also said the military has to keep functioning. The brigade is a living organism. So it keeps operating. People keep doing what they were doing to the best of their ability. But in our submission that does not lead to the inference that therefore Mr. Kubura controlled everyone, including those involved the detention facilities, because that's ultimately what we're talking about here, at all times before the 6th of August, 1993. General Karavelic also mentioned that Article 14 of the rules of service, which the Prosecution have relied upon, was not applicable in these circumstances, that it was applicable only in cases of emergency. For example, where a commander was killed or taken captive, then the deputy stands in for that time. But he said in respect of a situation like this where somebody is not there, they've gone abroad, in those circumstances it has to be properly regulated. And because it's not -- we say you can take it one step further. Because it's not, you cannot infer that Mr. Kubura, automatically, as the next senior officer, became the commander. There were many other, as Mr. Terzic noted, assistant commanders. They continued doing their duty as well. And he said that the chief of staff, together with the assistant commanders, continued to run the brigade as best as they could. The Prosecution should have, but we say they didn't, bring evidence to show that Mr. Kubura was able to and did issue orders particularly in respect of detention centres, in respect of the military police, in respect of any security matters relevant to the 7th Brigade. There is another big gap, another hole right there, and that applies to the Motel Sretno. They've asked Your Honours to infer his presence there, but they've also said you must infer that he could have done anything. It certainly applies to the music school as well, which I will address Your Honours on at a later point. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Your Honour, the Prosecution in their brief in the paragraphs that follow paragraph 57, they refer to some quotes of members of the 7th Brigade who testified before Your Honours. Mr. Junuzovic, for example, footnote 133. We would urge Your Honours to read all of what the 7th Brigade witnesses said. The Prosecution has chosen the one quote which does appear on its face to go against what I'm saying, but if you look at everything he said, the picture is different. There's another occasion where this happens, I will come to it later, in respect of international witnesses. If you take one paragraph from what they said, yes, it might appear to fly in the face of what the Defence is submitting to Your Honours, but when you look at the total picture, you look at the cross-examination and you look at how the witness was asked to expand and explore further aspects of the issue, that's when Your Honours get to the evidence that you can rely upon. And he made it quite clear - and this is at page 18501 and onwards - that Mr. Kubura was not signing any documents as the commander. He was doing so as the chief of staff, as he probably would have done in any event, even if the commander was there. None of these documents related to security matters, detention facility matters. He also said that in his practice he wasn't acting like the commander. People weren't referring to him as "our commander," as often happens in these situations where somebody assumes power in a vacuum. He didn't move into the commander's office. He was still in the office of the chief of staff. There are no indications on the evidence that we have somebody here beginning to take over, grooming himself for becoming the commander. Rather, we see Mr. Kubura continuing to do what he has always done as chief of staff. And likewise, the other assistant commanders are doing the same. And the brigade keeps functioning. It's a living organism. They all did the best that they could in those circumstances. In our submission, there cannot be a basis for criminal liability. Your Honours have to, on the evidence before Your Honours, be able to deduce that Mr. Kubura indeed did effectively control, he had actual control over the perpetrators, he himself. We say that only happens from 6 August onwards when his position is finally clarified. But up until then, he is not the person where the buck stops. Your Honour, I'm now going to move on to Miletici and Maline. I think it may be prudent if we had a short break at this stage, and I will then go on to those counts, together with addressing the music school, before I conclude. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I plan to complete the closing submission on behalf of Mr. Kubura by the normal break for lunch at quarter to two. It may be, although I don't think so, it may be that it goes a little longer than that, but I am informed that we do have this courtroom for the entire day, so if we ran a little bit over quarter to two that would not cause any major inconvenience, but I will aim to finish by the normal break. Your Honours, turning to Miletici and Maline. Mr. Mundis said in his closing that, and I quote his exact words: "The only reasonable inference that can be drawn from this evidence that you have before you is that these foreign fighters were under the effective command and control of Mr. Hadzihasanovic, and with respect to the foreigners in the 7th Brigade, under the effective command and control of Mr. Kubura." So he qualified it quite clearly. He said, "with respect to the foreigners in the 7th Brigade." What is, Your Honours, the evidence that Mr. Mundis was referring to? Firstly, he took Your Honours through a series of alleged joint combat operations in 1992 and 1993. In our submission, none of these incidents are at all relevant to the case against Mr. Kubura. He is not charged with any incidents in Karaula, for example, or any incidents in Bjelo Buce, or any incidents in Kacuni in June 1993, or Grabovica, or Novi Travnik, or Dubravica or Guca Gora. Mr. Kubura was under no obligation to prepare any defence in respect of any of these particular alleged incidents. He has not been charged with any crimes been committed there by persons the Prosecution allege are his subordinates. These various incidents have not even been mentioned in the indictment as connected to what happened in Miletici and Maline. We invite Your Honours to focus on those two villages and what happened on those days to determine whether the Prosecution has proved its case. In any event, many different brigades and units are mentioned in respect to these various incidents that the Prosecution showed Your Honours on that map with the dots on. The operations involved many different units, according to the Prosecution. There was no evidence in respect of any of them that there was incorporation into any brigade. In fact, by their very name which the Prosecution has chosen, "joint operations," they indicate a horizontal link more than something vertical, that of subordination within ranks. The Prosecution has not sought to show how any of them relate to the events in Miletici and Maline, and that's because in respect of those events they cannot prove that the 7th Brigade was even present, let alone involved in any joint combat operations with any foreign or other irregular troops. The other evidence that Mr. Mundis referred to was that of the international witnesses who the Prosecution have argued are credible witnesses because of the fact that they are independent, no axe to grind. They were there, the eyes and ears of the international community on the ground. Which is all very well, Your Honours, but everything depends on what actually did they see? What did they know? How much did they find out about what was happening within the warring factions? They've all agreed, Your Honours, that they knew very little. This was not their war. They were not gathering intelligence, and they had no hard evidence on who the foreigners were subordinated to. There were rumours, there were assertions, possibilities, probabilities. Those were all included in some of their reports, but nothing that would take Your Honours to a certain, beyond-reasonable-doubt conclusion. All of those international witnesses were brutally honest with Your Honours in saying that they could not be sure one way or another where the Mujahedin fitted in. They had theories, yes, because they had no hard evidence, hard intelligence about who controlled the Mujahedin. In any event, none of them were in Miletici or Maline at the time. They never witnessed what happened there, and they're not able to say who was in charge at the time. Mr. Mundis quoted a section from Mr. Williams' testimony for Your Honours. What wasn't cited was what he said in cross-examination when he was asked about Mujahedin in Central Bosnia. The question was put to him: "General Williams, you said in response to questions from Their Honours that the command and control situation was easier to assess between the formal units in Central Bosnia but more difficult with regard to the Mujahedin." And his answer at page 5998 was: "That's correct." The question continued: "And the reason for that would be that, as you've said on a number of occasions, you lacked hard intelligence about the subordination structure with respect to the Mujahedin." His answer: "Yes, that's true." When he was asked about Exhibit P378, about a sentence in that report saying Mujahedin are subsumed within the 7th Brigade, he said: "I think the statement made in that paragraph -" that's paragraph 15 of the exhibit - "may be a little too concrete given the evidence that was probably available at that time." The question continued: "The rest of the paragraph refers to a caveat of some sort which says that there are some independent Mujahedin units." And he says, "Yes, that is what it says." So he conceded that that kind of statement was too concrete given the real evidence that they had. Mr. Mundis also quoted Mr. Bower, but what was not highlighted to Your Honours is that at page 5126, he was asked whether he had any detailed knowledge of the structure of the 7th Brigade and the subordination and composition of that brigade, and he said, "Along with any other unit, no. I wasn't the military liaison officer." When the military liaison officer, one of them, Mr. Kijal [phoen], was questioned, he said exactly the same thing: "We didn't have that kind of information." With Mr. Bower the question was then put: "So you had no intelligence about under whose control the Mujahedin were, did you?" "Me personally? No." In our submission, Your Honour, that evidence, and Your Honours will see that increasingly in the international witnesses when they are examined, is highly pertinent to the issue in dispute. As independent observers, they were not certain. And likewise Your Honours, given their evidence, cannot be certain either, we say. There was lastly, Your Honours will recall, the evidence of Mr. Chambers where he was asked about a document prepared by him regarding the preparation of reports, and he said in that document, and he confirmed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that it was probably used for -- for briefing, that you could almost write anything in these reports. No one really checks. No one really cares. Now, that's not to say that all of these reports are wholly useless and inaccurate, but it's a telling remark as to how much reliance can be placed on these reports on the critical issues in this case, especially when the international witnesses have themselves conceded that they did not have the answers. Your Honour, in our submission it is also telling that when the Prosecution referred to various of these other incidents, these joint operations, as they put that, in their oral submission, they at great length went into examining the documents and in particular looking at the war diaries from the brigades that were operating in those areas. And yet when it comes to Miletici and Maline, that evidence about the documents on the ground, the war diaries, which have been shown to witnesses and which they have verified, has been totally pushed aside. Your Honours will know the Defence case for Mr. Kubura is that the 7th Brigade was not present in either of those locations, as is borne out by the witness testimony of all the brigades that were present and, most importantly, by contemporaneous documents and war diaries that have been shown to witnesses who were in the area at the time, mainly witnesses from the 306th Brigade. The Prosecution has not sought to deal with that evidence. In our submission, evidence which provides an entirely reasonable and rational inference that can be drawn of innocence, the Prosecution has to exclude all other reasonable inferences to convince Your Honours of guilt. In our view, they have not done that in respect of Maline and Miletici because there are inferences that can be drawn entirely reasonably which point in the opposite direction. It is for the Prosecution to negative any other inferences that can be drawn. That is the burden that they carry. Not only must they show Your Honours that it is the only reasonable inference, but they also have to negative all other possible inferences that could be drawn which are reasonable and which point away from guilt. They haven't, for example, dealt with General Reinhardt, who was their own witness who categorically stated that he did not find any evidence of the 7th Brigade being present in Miletici or Maline. They have not dealt with the evidence relating to Mr. Ramo Durmis. That is, if Your Honours look at the written submissions, the only evidence that they really rely upon in respect of Mr. Kubura for Miletici, that Mr. Durmis was still a part, as they say, of the 7th Brigade at that time. And yet a Prosecution exhibit, P941, which was a statement taken from Mr. Durmis as a suspect, confirms in his own words that he left the brigade before any of those alleged incidents. He says that himself. And Your Honours will remember questions that were asked of Judge Ahmetovic about that statement. Not the substance of it but the form that it took. That's at page 16193 onwards. Whether it was taken in accordance with the law, that he was properly cautioned and that he was able to make his statement voluntarily. And he said yes, the statement was perfectly lawful. The Prosecution have also overlooked DK29, a document dated 19 February 1993, which quite plainly shows that the commander of the 1st Company of the 1st Battalion is not Mr. Durmis in February 1993. In his interview to Witness ZP, he said the same. He didn't say when he'd left, but he said he had left. That corresponds with this evidence that he gave in P914 and also DK29. You've heard from the witnesses within the 7th Brigade - Mr. Terzic, Mr. Adilovic, Mr. Abramovic, Mr. Jusufovic - who all were either with Mr. Durmis at the time or knew him. This is firsthand evidence they gave of how he left the brigade after the operations in December 1992. This evidence wasn't challenged by the Prosecution. There is no reason to, in our submission, disbelieve the evidence that these witnesses gave, which is entirely consistent with what Mr. Durmis himself said and the documents that I have referred to. Yes, there is the citation on 14 April 1993. That's P727, but the witnesses have clarified that that relates to the operations in 1992, at the end of 1992, that the citations were given on the 14th of April because that was the one-year anniversary, as is stated in the document, of the formation of the Bosnian army. And it's quite clear if you read the way in which the award is given, that it's not given to Mr. Durmis himself. It's given to the 1st Company. There is a section in the document where the persons who are awarded individually and personally are listed, and then there's a separate section where the 1st Company is mentioned. But in any event, he is no longer part of the brigade at that point. Any later references to him, none of them confirm that he's still with the brigade. They all show that he is outside of the brigade, that he is no longer under the effective control of that brigade or any other. He is one of the renegades, in our submission, that Mr. Sipic is referring to in various of his documents where he complains about problems with people who are no longer part of a brigade, where their status must be resolved. We have in our brief referred extensively to those documents, because Mr. Sipic was here before Your Honours. It was his area of responsibility, and he was able to testify as to what happened within his area. At no point did he ever maintain that the 7th Brigade were involved in any of the alleged killings. And also, he confirmed through looking at his documents that there was no reference to the 7th Brigade in relation to any of those alleged killings. Mr. Sipic made many complaints, as Your Honours will see from those documents. There was always something being sent up to the corps command, but in none of those documents did he ever say the 7th Brigade is involved here in the commission of crimes and something must be done about that. And Your Honours might think he had every reason. If there was another brigade committing crimes in his area of responsibility, he had every reason to cover himself and report that. He has no interest in protecting any other brigade. But there's no document that indicates the 7th Brigade was there and involved and in any way needed to be investigated. His complaints are about Mujahedin, and he mentions people who have left brigades. Moreover, as Mr. Waespi said when he summed up the reporting that was going on after these incidents, there was no mention in any of those reports about the 7th Brigade being responsible for any of these incidents. The Prosecution may have alleged wrongly some form of cover-up, but they have not alleged that there was a cover-up for the 7th Brigade. That's because there was not anything of the sort. The reports do not mention that brigade. They certainly mention other brigades. They mention the 306th Brigade, but they do not mention the 7th Brigade. When Mr. Mazowiecki wanted a report, when the chains of gathering information and gathering reports was set in motion, the 7th Brigade was never approached at all in respect to incidents in Miletici and Maline. They weren't approached before that. There's no notice whatsoever to any of the commanders in the 7th Brigade of any problem being reported in respect of their brigade. Your Honour, I refer here for completeness to three exhibits, P111, P171, and P174, which support the submission that I have made. Your Honours, Mr. Mundis and his predecessor Mr. Withopf both referred you to this notion of a puzzle to prove their case. Mr. Mundis said some time ago - this was at page 4824 - that Your Honours are clearly being given small pieces of the puzzle which will only be clear at the end of the case. Likewise, Mr. Withopf, in April 2004, said: "I wish to really emphasise that this is a circumstantial case. At the end of the day, there will be many, many, many bits and pieces of evidence which, put together, will provide the Trial Chamber with the full picture, the full picture of the truth." Your Honours, if you consider paragraph 104 of our written closing brief, Your Honours will see in our submission what is a true piecing together of the puzzle of what happened. In our view, the Prosecution have not addressed this evidence. Starting with the testimony of Enver Adilovic, about his company going, after events in Ahmici, to an area near Vitez, arriving there on the 20th of April and remaining there until July. That was the so-called 4th Vitez Company of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Brigade. Not disputed in any way by the Prosecution. We then move on to DK20, dated 5 June 1993, which was confirmed by many witnesses. And it's a report from the Operational Group Bosanska Krajina sent to the 3rd Corps, stating that on the 4th of June, 1993, the HVO had intensified its attack and that there was an HVO artillery attack from the direction of Hajdarove Njive. By this report, Mr. Sipic is also ordered to move along the Maline axis. And also, very significantly, it is proposed in this report to the 3rd Corps Command that Ovnak should be attacked from Zenica. As you know, that indeed did happen on the 8th of June. The 2nd and the 3rd Battalions of the 7th Brigade were involved in that operation from the other end. But to complete the picture so Your Honours know where the 1st Battalion was on that day, we continue with further documents. This is P279 of 5 June, an order from the 306th Brigade -- sorry, an order to the 306th Brigade, also to the 3rd Corps Command, to continue with the operations in the Bila Valley. No mention is made of the 7th Brigade being in the Bila Valley at that time. Also on the same day, DK19, the OG reporting to the 3rd Corps command, which states that the 1st Battalion, not in the Bila Valley, but Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is engaged towards Hajdareve Njive where the HVO is holding firing positions. This is confirmed in the war diary of the Operational Group DK18. So not only is it a report that has gone out but it's confirmed as something that did happen on that day. Your Honours have been to this area and know its location in relation to the town of Travnik where the 1st Battalion of the 7th Brigade was based. It's very close, about a kilometre away, but some ten to 12 kilometres away from Maline. On the 6th of June, DK34. This is a report from the 1st Battalion of the 7th Brigade, stating that it has captured Hajdareve Njive but had to retreat. This was confirmed by witnesses from the 7th Brigade who actually participated in that operation. DK21. We've moved on now to the following day, the 7th of June. We see the 306th operational diary states that the HVO is shelling and attacking in the Bila Valley and that a meeting of the 306th Brigade is taking place in Mehurici. Nowhere in that diary is it stated that the 7th Brigade is going to be involved in any way. Instead, what you have on the 8th of June, a document that has been shown to many witnesses, is an OG combat report signed by Alagic which states that the 1st Battalion of the 7th Brigade is active at Hajdareve Njive and towards Bukovica. Once again confirmed by witnesses who were part of this operation. We see here the documents reflecting the testimony that witnesses have been giving. Also in relation to document P465, Your Honours heard the evidence of General Cuskic, the commander of the 17th Krajina Brigade, who was in the area at the time working very closely with General Alagic. And he confirmed Alagic's signature in respect of P465, and he confirmed the reliability of that document, because he was in the field, and he said, "Yes, that was the situation in the field on 8 June," and that General Alagic would have prepared it from that information. 9 June 1993, the day after the events in Maline. DK22, which is a cable from the 306th Brigade to the 3rd Corps Command stating that the brigade had reached the Maline axis on 8 June. Various witnesses from the 306th Brigade who came to testify confirmed that that is in fact the operation they were involved in. No mention of the 7th Brigade involved in that operation in any way whatsoever. On 9 June, to complete the puzzle, DK42, an OG combat report stating that the 1st Battalion of the 7th Brigade is to attack towards Srbica. Witnesses have confirmed they moved from Hajdareve Njive where they had conducted the second operation there on the 8th of June, to the 9th of June to a nearby location, another location that Your Honours would have viewed during the site visit. Nowhere near the area of Maline. In our submission, it is quite plain that the activities of the 7th Brigade, all of its battalions, are accounted for during this time. There is a perfectly reasonable inference to be drawn which points to the 7th Brigade not participating in any way in the operations, and most importantly, in any way in any of the crimes that may have been committed during that time. Your Honour, the evidence that the Prosecution has relied upon in respect of Maline are three witnesses who were called during the Prosecution case who they suggest identified certain members of the 7th Brigade in the area of Maline at the time. However you regard this evidence, none of those witnesses placed any of the members of the 7th Brigade they say might have been there at the scene where the killings allegedly occurred. None of them were witnesses to that event, identifying members of the 7th Brigade. And in addition to that, none of the evidence, in our submission, confirms that in fact what they saw were members of the 7th Brigade at the time. When their evidence is viewed as a whole, and we cited the evidence in full in our response to the Prosecution's 98 bis submission, it's plain that they either were not able to recognise the badges that they saw or didn't know the badges of the army or conceded that many different badges were seen or used by different people at the time and that they were not sure of who exactly was present there. Their testimony is not to be regarded as untruthful. That's not what we're suggesting. It's simply testimony that doesn't point with any certainty to the presence of any members of the 7th Brigade there, and it must be weighed up against the wealth of evidence that I've just outlined for Your Honours recorded in the documents and confirmed by the oral evidence of countless witnesses. This is evidence which the Prosecution have failed to address, and we say that you cannot therefore be certain, relying on three witnesses the Prosecution refers to whose evidence is not in any event clear given the case that the Defence for Mr. Kubura has put forward. The Prosecution has not built the puzzle filling in all the many, many, many pieces as they said they would. We have shown Your Honours what the true picture was both in respect of Miletici and Maline. In our submission, the case for Mr. Kubura to be acquitted on these counts is overwhelming. Your Honours, I want in the time remaining to make a few comments about the music school and the charges of destruction and looting in Ovnak which the Prosecution didn't have time to comment on in their submission. With respect to the music school, Your Honours, the key issue has always been what evidence was really available to Mr. Kubura of what was happening in the music school. It doesn't have to be evidence of actual beatings. It can be evidence which puts you on notice that further inquiries must be made. But there is nothing before Your Honours which shows that he was ever told anything about the music school. No reports, no meetings, no visits, no complaints made to him. He is an invisible figure when it comes to the music school. Many other people have been mentioned in relation to what went on there. Indeed, one of them is currently being prosecuted for what is happening there -- for what happened there. What the Prosecution are left to rely upon is this notion of a notorious or widespread rumour about the music school. We say that is not enough to infer knowledge on the part of Mr. Kubura. Firstly, there is evidence which contradicts that. Not all the witnesses that were called in respect of the music school indicated that these rumours were rife. The head of the Municipal Executive Committee for Zenica, for example, testified - and this is at page 14229 onwards - that if there were ongoing beatings and serious incidents at the music school on a daily basis, given the fact that it's located right in the centre of Zenica near the court, people would have known about this. Something would have been done. His view was that it was not something which everyone was aware of. Even Mr. Adamovic, who you heard from extensively in respect of the music school, acknowledged that he didn't know whether any of the rumours were true. There were rumours and stories, he said. "What the truth of the matter was I wouldn't be able to tell you." We say, Your Honours, on the basis of that kind of evidence and given the nature of the alleged offences there, it would be a bridge too far to therefore conclude that Mr. Kubura knew about what was happening. It would be one thing if the events there took place over an extended period of time and we were talking about hundreds and thousands of people being detained in concentrate camp-like facilities. It's in those circumstances that in cases like Yamashita and Toyoda, after the Second World War, the Tribunals said, look, these were just such big offences, so notorious, such awful events, that even though there was no report sent to you about it, you must have known. We are talking here about one small building. Your Honours went to the building. And this is not in any way to diminish the events that took place there and what persons may have had to endure there. Every single individual is entitled to have their body protected and not to be beaten in the way that we've heard some of the evidence come out. But we're talking about a limited number of people over a limited period of time. Even though the indictment says until January 1994, essentially by July there are no further allegations of any beatings. But in circumstances where you're talking about one venue in the context of the whole of Central Bosnia and the area where the 7th Brigade was operating, to infer knowledge on the basis that some witnesses have said there were some rumours and other witnesses have said no, they weren't that notorious, would, in our submission, be taking the principle of imputed knowledge to the extreme. In our submission, Your Honours would need to have at least some evidence of information flowing within the 7th Brigade command and to Mr. Kubura about what happened. Nobody from the international community spoke to him about this matter. He was not seen as the person to turn to. No one asked him for permission to visit the music school. He was not the authority in respect of the music school. He never went there with anyone. In fact, most of the international witnesses said they didn't even know who Mr. Kubura was. In our submission, the Prosecution is scratching at straws here in an attempt to try and get this charge to stick in respect of Mr. Kubura. In addition to that, I have to refer back to the points I made earlier on about his real ability, even if it can be inferred that he had knowledge, his real ability to do anything in respect of the music school. As the chief of staff, was it his responsibility at all, or what could he have done? And you have to layer onto that the evidence that has been led about the parallel security chain of command. Not that that is a chain of command which means that the security system is independent of the commander. We're not alleging that. What we're saying is that there was a separate chain of command for security matters, a chain of command that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. everyone would have been aware of who would have been dealing with these kinds of matters. And in circumstances where you're not the de jure commander but you do have an assistant for security matters, Your Honours might think that Mr. Kubura, even if he knew anything, would have been entirely reasonable in assuming that that matter was being dealt with by the assistant commander and the hierarchy above him and that he didn't have the power, without being formally assigned, to interfere, especially when -- and you have to layer on top of that that there was evidence about people using the music school as a way of getting money, as a way of taking revenge, that you had some very powerful people there doing their own thing. So, Your Honours, we ask you to take all of those various layers into account. Firstly, lack of evidence of knowledge; secondly, lack of evidence of control in respect of the persons in the music school; also, to take into account the security chain of command which was operational at the time; and in addition to that, fourthly, you have evidence about people doing these things for their own personal gain with, Your Honours might think, incentive to cover up what was happening there. We say there must at least be doubt regarding whether the Prosecution have proved this case. Do all of those layers not add up to a degree of doubt to the point where we would say Your Honours cannot be certain enough to convict in respect of the music school. Lastly, there is the ongoing proceedings against Mr. Isic. No one else has been proceeded against from the group of people I've mentioned who were intimately involved with the music school. He is the person who has been singled out. And Your Honours might well think that the fact that he is being punished, albeit sometime after the event, is important, that the person most responsible is being brought to justice, and that that should at least serve, at the very least serve, as compelling mitigation in respect of this particular charge. Your Honour, finally I come to Ovnak. Your Honours would have heard the evidence from witnesses in the 7th Brigade about what happened in Ovnak. There is no evidence before Your Honours that members of the 7th Brigade were involved in operations outside of the mountain pass area of Ovnak and leading up to the Strmac elevation. Your Honours heard firsthand evidence of how people from the lowest level to the highest level of the battalion command, in a detailed way, and they set out how they were involved in this particular operation, that they didn't go to any of the other towns that are mentioned; Grahovici, Barakovici, and Susanj. There's no evidence that places any of them there. And how they withdrew immediately once the operation had been completed, as they were dispatched immediately for another operation in the area of Kakanj. The documents once again confirming that. This is not just the witnesses but the orders, the reports, and the war diaries. Once again, we say the bits of the puzzle fit together in respect of the case that the Defence has advanced. There is no evidence which pinpoints particular perpetrators being from the 7th Brigade, bearing in mind once again that this was a multi-brigade operation, being involved in either looting or destruction. As occurred in Vares, there is evidence that there was looting that took place over a long period of time. In Ovnak, the situation was the same, and we've seen pictures of houses destroyed, but no proof, we say, that that occurred on the 8th of June, because that would have to be the time frame that the Prosecution would have to show it occurred in, because after that the 7th Brigade was gone, something the Prosecution haven't challenged. So it would have to be in that limited time period that that destruction and looting occurred. Thereafter, those persons were not the subordinates of Mr. Kubura. So with Ovnak again, it comes down to the problem that has always haunted the Prosecution in this case: Who are the perpetrators? We don't need names and addresses, but they have to show they are the subordinates of Mr. Kubura. Your Honours, if I may now move on to our concluding remarks. I mentioned earlier the ICRC study on customary international law. They have set out a series of rules that they say have become part of customary law based on the practice of states and of the international community. Rule 153 is the rule on command responsibility which mirrors the provision in the Statute of the ICTY and the ICC. In the commentary where commander/subordinate relationship is addressed, the ICRC had the following to say: "The relationship between the commander and the subordinate does not necessarily need to be a direct de jure one. The international tribunals identified the actual possession of control over the actions of subordinates, in the sense of the material to prevent and punish the commission of crimes, is the crucial criterion." So it's the actual possession of control over the actions of subordinates. That is the touchstone for this entire case. We would take it one step further to say it's the actual possession of control in respect of the identified perpetrators when you're looking at implementing this in the context of criminal trial. We as the Defence accept that it is difficult to prove actual possession of control and that circumstantial evidence is, therefore, going to have to be invoked in many cases. Not only in this case but in other cases before the international court. However, in our submission, Article 7(3) is not a licence to lower the standard of proof. Even though the accused didn't directly commit the crime, as it is alleged, of murder, the charge is still one of murder, a very serious offence, and only, we say, the clearest evidence and the clearest conclusions drawn upon that evidence can be relied upon by Your Honours. In that way, we can honour the very high standards of international criminal law which have been founded in the judgement of Nuremberg where there were acquittals on this very principle, and indeed before the ICTY. Your Honours, in a colloquial sentence, we say the case against Mr. Kubura is just not there. It has not been put together or proved beyond reasonable doubt. However the Prosecution has tried to stretch and squeeze and push together, the leaks and the holes remain. When you unpick it bit by bit and you look at what is really underneath the allegations, we say it's just not there. That is why we ask Your Honours to let Mr. Kubura walk out of here a free man. Thank you, Your Honours.
